Mixed graphical models with the psychnets R package

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland
Source: vignettes/mixed-graphical-models.Rmd
mixed-graphical-models.Rmd

When several measures of motivation, learning strategies and well-being are analysed together, which associations remain after accounting for the other variables? A graphical model addresses this question by representing constructs as nodes and their conditional associations as edges, rather than treating each construct as an isolated outcome (Borsboom et al., 2021). A correlation network displays pairwise relationships, whereas a graphical model seeks to distinguish conditional relationships from associations that may be explained by other measured variables. This can help applied researchers describe how related psychological and educational characteristics are organised. However, an estimated edge does not on its own demonstrate causality, and conclusions also depend on the accuracy and stability of the estimated associations (Epskamp et al., 2018).

Educational applications have used psychological networks to examine the interplay of processes involved in learning. For example, networks have been applied to monitoring events during regulated learning (Malmberg et al., 2022) and to the relationships and temporal dynamics of self-regulation in academic writing (Saqr et al., 2021). More broadly, psychological network methods provide a way to study complex learning processes in which several constructs may be mutually related rather than arranged in a single sequence of predictors and outcomes (Saqr et al., 2024). The choice of network model should nevertheless reflect the variables collected and the research question. Models of moderation, for instance, address whether an association differs according to another variable, which is distinct from the pairwise associations estimated here (Haslbeck et al., 2021).

A practical difficulty is that the same study may include continuous scale scores, such as motivation or self-efficacy, and binary indicators, such as whether a learner completed a course or reported a particular behaviour. A Gaussian graphical model assumes continuous variables, whereas an Ising model is designed for binary variables. Neither directly accommodates both types without changing how some variables are represented. A mixed graphical model (Haslbeck & Waldorp, 2020) allows continuous and categorical variables to appear in the same network. It estimates a regression for each node using a model appropriate to that node’s type and combines the estimates to obtain edges. An edge indicates a conditional association given the other modelled variables, not evidence of an effect or a direction of influence.

This article demonstrates the approach using three continuous and two binary indicators related to self-regulated learning. It explains how the package estimates the network, how to interpret its edges and numerical diagnostics, and how to assess node centrality and predictability using measures suited to each variable type. It also compares two rules for combining the nodewise regressions and outlines what to report and what to consider before applying the method to educational or psychological data.

library(psychnets)

The model

A mixed graphical model represents conditional associations through a pairwise Markov random field,

p(x1,…,xp)∝exp⁡(∑jϕj(xj)+∑j<kϕjk(xj,xk)), p(x_1, \ldots, x_p) \propto \exp\left(\sum_j \phi_j(x_j) + \sum_{j<k}\phi_{jk}(x_j, x_k)\right),

Here, a zero pairwise term ϕjk\phi_{jk} indicates that xjx_j and xkx_k are conditionally independent given all other variables in the model. Estimation proceeds one node at a time. For node jj, the coefficients 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta minimise

1n∑i=1nℓ(xij,β0+𝐱i,−j𝖳𝛃)+λj‖𝛃‖1, \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \ell\left(x_{ij}, \beta_0 + \mathbf{x}_{i,-j}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta\right) + \lambda_j\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1 ,

The loss ℓ\ell is the Gaussian or binomial negative log-likelihood, depending on the node type. The ℓ1\ell_1 penalty can shrink coefficients to zero, giving a network with fewer edges. The penalty λj\lambda_j is selected separately for each node using the extended BIC (γ=0.25\gamma = 0.25 by default). Selected coefficients below a small sample-size-dependent threshold are also set to zero (threshold = "LW", as in mgm). Continuous variables are standardised so that their original units do not determine the coefficients. Because each pair of variables appears in two nodewise regressions, two estimates must be combined. The AND rule retains an edge only when both regressions select it; the OR rule retains it when either does. The edge weight is the mean of the two estimates.

By default, the function infers node types from the data. Factor and character columns, along with numeric columns containing at most 10 distinct integer values, are treated as categorical; other numeric columns are treated as Gaussian. In this example, the two 0/1 indicators are binary and the three scores are Gaussian. The function issues a warning when the integer-value rule classifies a numeric column as categorical. Researchers should check these classifications against their measurement design and use types to override them when necessary.

Data

SRL_GPT holds 300 sets of responses to the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire. The responses were generated by a large language model (GPT) in a study of how such models answer psychological surveys (Vogelsmeier et al., 2025); they serve as a well-structured example and are not evidence about students. To obtain variables of both types, two of the five construct scores are recoded as binary indicators.

  • Continuous nodes: CSU (cognitive strategy use), IV (intrinsic value) and SE (self-efficacy), construct scores on a scale from 1 to 7.
  • Binary nodes: SR_hi, 1 when self-regulation is at or above its median; TA_hi, 1 when test anxiety is at or above its median.
  • Observations: one row per respondent; the data are complete.
mixed_data <- transform(SRL_GPT,
                        SR_hi = as.integer(SR >= median(SR)),
                        TA_hi = as.integer(TA >= median(TA)),
                        SR = NULL, TA = NULL)
head(mixed_data)
#>        CSU       IV       SE SR_hi TA_hi
#> 1 5.307692 5.666667 5.777778     0     1
#> 2 5.846154 6.444444 6.000000     1     1
#> 3 6.615385 6.666667 6.222222     1     0
#> 4 5.692308 6.555556 6.333333     1     1
#> 5 4.384615 5.555556 4.888889     0     1
#> 6 4.846154 5.444444 5.666667     0     0

The median splits are used solely to demonstrate a mixed-variable analysis. They discard differences between observations within each category and should not be taken as recommended data preparation. In an applied study, a continuous measure should generally remain continuous unless the binary states have a substantive or measurement-based justification.

Which variables are directly associated?

psychnet() with method = "mgm" estimates the network with the AND rule.

mixed_net <- psychnet(data = mixed_data, method = "mgm")
summary(mixed_net)
#> <psychnet> mgm network
#>   nodes: 5   edges: 6   (undirected)
#>   optimality (KKT residual): 2.59e-11
#>   edge weight: range [0.198, 0.649], mean 0.420
as.data.frame(mixed_net)
#>   from    to    weight
#> 1  CSU    IV 0.5186459
#> 2  CSU    SE 0.4857298
#> 3   IV    SE 0.1975632
#> 4  CSU SR_hi 0.4674247
#> 5   IV SR_hi 0.6487223
#> 6   SE SR_hi 0.2038918

The fitted network contains 6 edges, all positive, with weights ranging from 0.198 to 0.649. The largest weight links intrinsic value and high self-regulation (0.649). Conditional on the other measured variables, higher intrinsic value is associated with greater likelihood of belonging to the higher self-regulation category. Cognitive strategy use is connected to intrinsic value (0.519), self-efficacy (0.486) and high self-regulation (0.467). High test anxiety has no selected edges under the AND rule. This means that none of its potential edges was retained by both nodewise regressions, not that test anxiety is unrelated to learning in general.

The coefficients for continuous–continuous, continuous–binary and binary–binary pairs do not all share the same scale. Consequently, their magnitudes should be compared primarily within the same pair type. For a binary–binary edge, the sign of the logistic coefficient is kept; some software reports only its magnitude, because that sign depends on how the categories are coded.

Is the fitted network the optimum of its objective?

Each penalised regression is fitted by an iterative optimisation procedure. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions provide a numerical check on whether the fitted coefficients satisfy the objective’s optimality conditions. The certificate reports the largest residual across the nodewise regressions; a value close to zero indicates that the numerical solution satisfies these conditions to high precision.

certificate(mixed_net)
#>   method  certificate kind certified
#> 1    mgm 2.589419e-11  kkt      TRUE

The reported residual is 2.59×10−112.59 \times 10^{-11}, and the fitted solution is certified. This supports the numerical convergence of the penalised regressions, but says nothing about whether the same edges would be selected in another sample or whether the underlying constructs have been measured reliably.

Which variables are most connected?

net_centralities() returns strength, the sum of absolute edge weights, and expected influence, the signed sum.

net_centralities(mixed_net)
#>    node  strength expected_influence
#> 1   CSU 1.4718004          1.4718004
#> 2    IV 1.3649314          1.3649314
#> 3    SE 0.8871848          0.8871848
#> 4 SR_hi 1.3200388          1.3200388
#> 5 TA_hi 0.0000000          0.0000000

Cognitive strategy use has the highest strength (1.472), followed by intrinsic value (1.365) and high self-regulation (1.320). Because every selected edge is positive, expected influence is identical to strength for all nodes. High test anxiety has a value of 0 on both measures, consistent with its isolation in this fitted network. These descriptive rankings require caution: combining weights from different types of edges makes centrality across continuous and binary nodes only approximately comparable. High centrality also does not, by itself, identify a suitable intervention target.

How well is each variable predicted by the others?

Predictability uses a measure suited to each node type: R2R^2 for continuous nodes, and for binary nodes the normalized classification accuracy, nCC⁡j=(CC⁡j−mj)/(1−mj)\operatorname{nCC}_j = (\operatorname{CC}_j - m_j)/(1 - m_j), where CC⁡j\operatorname{CC}_j is the proportion classified correctly and mjm_j the proportion in the larger category (Haslbeck & Waldorp, 2018). net_predict() needs the data to compute both.

net_predict(mixed_net, data = mixed_data)
#>    node     type metric predictability accuracy
#> 1   CSU gaussian     R2      0.8131598       NA
#> 2    IV gaussian     R2      0.7757803       NA
#> 3    SE gaussian     R2      0.7153497       NA
#> 4 SR_hi   binary    nCC      0.7391304     0.88
#> 5 TA_hi   binary    nCC      0.0000000     0.50

For the continuous nodes, the fitted models account for approximately 81% of the observed variance in cognitive strategy use (R2=0.813R^2 = 0.813), 78% in intrinsic value (R2=0.776R^2 = 0.776) and 72% in self-efficacy (R2=0.715R^2 = 0.715). For high self-regulation, classification accuracy is 88%, corresponding to a normalised classification accuracy of 0.739 after adjustment for the majority-category baseline. High test anxiety has 50% accuracy and an nCC of 0, indicating no improvement over that baseline. All these values are calculated on the data used to fit the network and should not be interpreted as performance on new observations.

Does the edge-combination rule change the network?

The two regressions of a pair can disagree. With rule = "OR" a pair is kept when either regression selects it.

mixed_or <- psychnet(data = mixed_data, method = "mgm", rule = "OR")
summary(mixed_or)
#> <psychnet> mgm network
#>   nodes: 5   edges: 7   (undirected)
#>   optimality (KKT residual): 2.59e-11
#>   edge weight: range [-0.186, 0.649], mean 0.334
as.data.frame(mixed_or)
#>    from    to     weight
#> 1   CSU    IV  0.5186459
#> 2   CSU    SE  0.4857298
#> 3    IV    SE  0.1975632
#> 4   CSU SR_hi  0.4674247
#> 5    IV SR_hi  0.6487223
#> 6    SE SR_hi  0.2038918
#> 7 SR_hi TA_hi -0.1861295

The OR network contains 7 edges. The 6 edges retained under the AND rule have unchanged weights, while one additional negative edge links high self-regulation to high test anxiety (-0.186). Conditional on the three continuous constructs, higher-category self-regulation is associated with lower likelihood of higher-category test anxiety. However, only one of the two nodewise regressions selected this edge. Its presence therefore depends on the combination rule, unlike the other six edges. Comparing the rules makes this modelling choice visible rather than treating the additional association as an unequivocal finding.

What does the network look like?

cograph::splot() draws the network, with green positive and red negative edges and a ring showing each node’s predictability.

cograph::splot(mixed_net, psych_styling = TRUE, predictability = TRUE)

The figure shows four connected nodes and an isolated high test anxiety node with an empty predictability ring. Node positions come from a layout algorithm and carry no statistical meaning.

Reporting the analysis

For reproducibility, a report should identify the variables and their node types, explain how binary categories were defined, and state the sample size, the value of γ\gamma, the edge-combination rule and the handling of missing data. It should also give the selected edge weights and report predictability using R2R^2 for continuous nodes and normalised classification accuracy for binary nodes. Any sensitivity to the combination rule should be reported alongside the primary network.

For this illustrative dataset of 300 complete, LLM-generated responses, the mixed graphical model comprised three continuous and two binary nodes. The AND rule retained 6 positive edges, the largest between intrinsic value and high self-regulation (0.649), and left high test anxiety isolated. The OR rule additionally retained a negative edge between high self-regulation and high test anxiety (-0.186). These findings describe the generated responses, not associations established in a sample of learners.

Assumptions and when to use a mixed graphical model

  • The model is for data that combine continuous and binary variables. With continuous variables only, a Gaussian graphical model is simpler; with binary variables only, the Ising model.
  • Continuous nodes are modelled by linear regression, binary nodes by logistic regression, and observations are independent of one another.
  • Categorical variables with more than two levels require native = FALSE, which fits a multinomial regression through the optional glmnet package and keeps the variable as one node. One-hot coding is not an equivalent alternative, because it turns one variable into several nodes.
  • An edge retained only under the OR rule is sensitive to the combination rule and merits more cautious interpretation than an edge retained by both.
  • Edges are conditional associations, not causal effects.
